But why is the tray still in the room? When were the trays taken away from the rooms of Harriet Sipper and Richard Nigges?" [272] "They might not have ordered anything," I said. "They might have just ordered drinks - tea and sherry - so there was no tray to begin with. And Ada Gransberry brought a lot of clothes, twice as many as the other two. Look, there's not even room for another petticoat in the wardrobe." [273] "You're right," said Poirot. "Lazari said they all ordered dinner, and we'll check later what each of them specifically ordered. I wouldn't have overlooked this if I hadn't been worried about Jenny. I still don't know where Jenny is! And Jenny is about the same age as these three victims, between forty and forty-five years old." [274] While Poirot checked their mouths and cufflinks, I turned my face away. He checked them, occasionally exclaiming in various ways. I looked at the fireplace and out the window from time to time, trying to avoid thinking again about the hands that would never have to be held again. I even thought about my crossword puzzle, where I had made a mistake. [275] After checking the three rooms, Poirot insisted on returning to the third floor, room 238, where Richard Nigges was. Perhaps going to the rooms of the victims so many times won't make me feel uncomfortable? So far, the answer is still no. As I entered Nigges' room again, it felt like I was being forced to climb a treacherous mountain, and I knew beforehand that reaching the summit would lead to disaster. [276] Poirot did not notice my distress, and I hoped it was because I had covered it up and not attracted his attention. He stood in the middle of the room and said to me, "My friend, this room is the most different, isn't it? Indeed, Miss Edith Garnet's room has an extra teacup and tray, but here there is a sherry glass, no teacup, and a window that is completely open, while the windows in the other two rooms are closed. It's cold in Mr. Nix's room!" [277] "Lazari found the body in this room just like this," I said, "without any changes." [278] Poirot walked to the open window and said, "This is the beautiful view that Lazari wanted to show me, the hotel garden. Miss Harriet Sippel and Miss Edith Garnet's rooms are on the other side of the hotel, where you can see 'Great London.' Can you see those trees, Kattimer?" [279] I told him I had seen them, wondering if he thought I was an idiot for not seeing the trees right by the window. [280] "Another difference in this room is the position of the cufflinks," said Poirot. "Did you notice? Miss Harriet Sippel and Miss Edith Garnet's cufflinks were in their mouths, slightly protruding from their lips. While Richard Nix's cufflinks were very deep inside, almost at his throat." [281] I opened my mouth to object, then gave up, but it was too late, Poirot saw the denial in my eyes. So he asked, "What do you want to say?" [282] "I think you're being too rigid," I said. "The three victims all had a cufflink with the initials PIJ in their mouths, which is a common point, not a different one. The position of the cufflink in the mouth is not a big issue." [283] "This is a huge difference! The lips and throat are different positions, completely different!" Poirot came over to me and stood in front of me, continuing, "Katchuk, please remember this: when three murders are almost identical, every tiny detail is crucial." [284] Do I really have to remember this pearl of wisdom, even though I don't agree with it? However, Poirot need not worry, I remember everything he has said to me, word for word, and the more he angers me, the better I remember. [285] "All three victims had cufflinks in their mouths," I repeated stubbornly, "and that's enough for me." [286] "I understand," Poirot said with disappointment. "It's enough for you, and it's probably enough for the hundreds of people under you, and I have no doubt it's enough for your superiors and Scotland Yard. But for Hercule Poirot, it's not enough!" [287] I had to remind myself that Poirot was talking about the similarities and differences in the case, not me. [288] "What about the open windows?" he asked me. "The windows in the other two rooms were closed. Is that not important?" [289] "Maybe it doesn't matter," I said. "Richard Nigges might have opened this room's window himself, and there was no reason for the killer to close it. Poirot, you often say that even in the winter, British people like to open windows because we believe it's good for the body." [290] "My friend," Poirot said patiently, "consider this: it is impossible for the three people not to have been poisoned, to have fallen naturally from the armchair and lie flat on the floor with their hands by their sides and their feet pointing towards the door. Why didn't anyone crawl across the room? Why didn't anyone fall on the other side of the chair? The killer rearranged their bodies to ensure that each corpse was in the same position, at the same distance from the chair and the small table. So, since the killer went to such lengths to make the three crime scenes identical, why didn't he close this room's window too? Perhaps Richard Nigges opened the window himself, but why didn't the killer close it to keep it consistent with the other two rooms' windows?" [291] I had to think about this. Poirot was right; the bodies had been arranged intentionally to make them look identical. [292] The bodies arranged neatly...
[293] "I think it depends on where you draw the line for the crime scene," I said, trying to pull myself back to the darkest room I had ever experienced. "It depends on whether you include the window or not." [294] "Draw the line for the crime scene?" [295] "Yes, not literally, but theoretically. Perhaps, the killer only created a small crime scene here." [296] Poirot chuckles, trying to hide his smile with his small mustache. "A theoretically defined crime scene. Ah, I see. Where does the crime scene begin and where does it end? That's indeed a question. Can it be smaller than this room? It's an interesting question for philosophers." [297] "Thank you." [298] "You're welcome. Carstairs, tell me, what do you think happened at the Blaxland Hotel last night? Let's put aside the motive for a moment and talk about what you think the killer did? First, second, third, like that." [299] "I don't know." [300] "Think carefully, Carstairs." [301] "Hmm... I think he came to the hotel, pocketed the cufflinks, and went to these three rooms in order. He probably went to Room 317 first, Ada Grantsberry's room, and then went downstairs, so he could leave the hotel quickly after killing the last person – Harryette Sipper in Room 121 on the second floor. If he went down one more floor, he could easily escape." [302] "So, what did he do in these three rooms?" [303] I sighed and said, "You already know the answer. He killed them, arranged the bodies neatly, put a cufflink in each mouth, locked the doors, and left." [304] "Did he encounter any obstacles when entering each room? Did each victim have a drink prepared for him, waiting to be poisoned – and were the drinks delivered at 7:15 by the hotel staff? Did he stand by the victim's side, watching them drink the poison, and then stand there waiting for them to die? Did he have dinner with one of them, and did Ada Grantsberry order him a cup of tea? All these actions – going to three rooms, killing three people, putting cufflinks in their mouths, arranging the bodies in a straight line with their feet facing the door – could all be done in the time between 7:15 and 8:10? My dear friend, it's impossible, completely impossible." [305] "You're right. Poirot, do you have a more reasonable explanation? After all, that's why you're here – to find a more reasonable explanation. You can start explaining whenever you want." As soon as I said these words, I regretted it, feeling too impulsive. [306] "I've already started." Hercule said, thankfully not sounding angry. "You said the killer left a note on the front desk saying he killed someone. Show it to me." [307] I took the note out of my pocket and handed it to him. John Good, the model employee mentioned by Lazare, found the note on the front desk at 8:20 last night. It read, "May they rest in peace, 121, 238, 317." [308] "This killer, or accomplice, had the audacity to approach the hotel's front desk, where he could have been seen by witnesses with the note in his hand. He was so bold and confident that he didn't sneak out through the back door." Hercule said. "He was really daring and confident." [309] "After Lazare saw the note, he immediately checked these three rooms and found their bodies. He even boasted to me that he checked all the rooms in the hotel afterwards. Luckily, all the other guests were unharmed." I said, although I knew I shouldn't say such unprofessional things. If Hercule were British, I would try to control my emotions better. [310] "I know I shouldn't say this, but I feel better after saying it. If Hercule were British, I might try to control my emotions better." [311] "Mr. Lazari would think the killer is among the guests, right? No, he wouldn't, the guests staying at the Brawnsham Hotel are all of high moral character and integrity!" [312] I coughed and tilted my head towards the door. Poirot turned around and saw Lazari standing at the door. He looked very happy and said, "Yes, that's right, Poirot sir." [313] "Everyone who was in the hotel on Thursday must come to Mr. Kitchbull's place to explain their whereabouts," Poirot said sternly to him. "Everyone, every guest, every employee, everyone who was in the hotel that day." [314] "I'm at your service, Mr. Kitchbull, you can talk to whoever you want," Lazari said respectfully to me. "Once we clean up the leftovers from breakfast, the restaurant will be yours to use. Feel free to have them all gathered there." [315] "Thank you. And I'll check those three rooms thoroughly again," said Poirot. I was surprised, as they had already been checked. "Kitchbull, find out where Harryt Westphal, Ada Grantsberry, and Richard Nigges live; which hotel employee booked their rooms; what food and drinks they ordered; and who delivered them to their rooms when." [316] I got up to leave, afraid he would keep giving me more tasks. [317] I had gone, he called after me, "See if there is a woman named Jeanne in the hotel, or working here." [318] "There is no Jeanne in the Bluxton Hotel, Mr. Poirot," Lazari said. "You should ask me, not Mr. Katchadourian. I know everyone here, the Bluxton Hotel is a happy family!" [319] * * *
[320] [1] In Britain, the first floor refers to the second floor. Therefore, Miss Harry Westbury's room, number 121, is actually on the second floor. In all instances where floors and room numbers are mentioned, the first number is increased by one to indicate the floor on which the room is located. [321] Chapter 4
[322] The crime scene expands
[323] Sometimes, recalling something someone said months or years ago can still make you laugh. For me, it was what Poirot said to me later that afternoon. He said, "Even the most clever detective would be at a loss when facing Mr. Lazari. If you don't praise him enough, he'll add on his own; as long as you keep flattering him, he'll patiently listen." [324] But Poirot finally succeeded in convincing Lazari to leave and let him check Room 238 alone. Lazari left without closing the door, and Poirot went over to close it and breathed a sigh of relief. It was much easier to think clearly without anyone else talking. [325] He walked straight to the window and stared out, pondering. Perhaps the killer had opened the window to escape, climbing down the tree after killing Nigus. [326] Why escape in this way? Why not exit normally through the corridor? Maybe the killer heard someone talking outside Nigel's room and didn't want to take the risk of being seen when leaving? Yes, that's possible. But when he casually walked to the front desk, placing the note on the table and claiming to have killed three people, why wasn't he afraid of being seen? Doing so would not only be seen but also potentially caught with evidence that could convict him on the spot. [327] Poirot looked at the corpse on the floor again, with no metallic glint on his lips. Out of the three victims, only Richard Nigel's cufflinks were on his throat, which was a bit unusual. There were many unusual things about this room. Therefore, Poirot decided to re-examine room 238 first. He... no need to deny it, he indeed suspected this room. Out of the three rooms, he liked this one the least. There was some disorder here, out of line. [328] Poirot stood by Nigel's corpse, frowning. Even by his standards, an open window did not suffice to say that the room was disordered. What made him feel this way? He slowly turned around, taking another look at the room. No, he must have been mistaken.
